pos: n. (defilement; the state of being made unclean; rendering Hebrew niddah and Greek miasma)
etymology: Latin pollutio, from polluere, to defile. The Greek miasma is a stain that spreads by contact — the word from which the medical sense comes.
biblical_def: Pollution is defilement, and Scripture uses it of things, of persons, and of a whole religion. Ezekiel indicts Jerusalem: “in thee have they humbled her that was set apart for pollution” (Eze 22:10). Peter of the apostate: “if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning” (2Pe 2:20). The Jerusalem council writes to the Gentiles “that they abstain from pollutions of idols” (Act 15:20). Malachi charges the priests: “ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar” (Mal 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pollution as the act of polluting; defilement; uncleanness; in a religious sense, the rendering of any thing unclean or unfit for sacred use; guilt, the effect of sin.
webster_full: POLLUTION, n. The act of polluting.
2. Defilement; uncleanness; impurity; the state of being polluted.
3. In the Jewish economy, legal or ceremonial uncleanness, which disqualified a person for sacred services or for common intercourse with the people.
4. Guilt; the effect of sin.
scriptures: For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.
But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.
Mal 1:7
Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible.
In thee have they discovered their fathers' nakedness: in thee have they humbled her that was set apart for pollution.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Defilement is treated as an outward accident, and the Lord said it is what comes out of a man that defiles him.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pharisees' whole system assumed that pollution travels inward — by the hands, the dish, the corpse, the Gentile — and the Lord reversed the direction in one sentence: “there is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man” (Mar 7:15), and then listed them, evil thoughts, adulteries, murders, covetousness, pride, foolishness. That does not abolish the category of defilement; it relocates its source. A man cannot be kept clean by controlling what touches him, because the contamination is already inside and is coming out.

Second Peter 2:20 shows what the relocation costs the doctrine of reformation. Men had escaped the pollutions of the world through knowledge of Christ — a real escape, a real change of life — and were again entangled and overcome, and the latter end was worse than the beginning. Escape from pollution is not the same as cleansing from it; the washed sow returns to the mire because she is a sow. What is needed is not distance from the defiling thing but a new nature, and only one thing does that.

James 1:27 keeps the word from becoming a doctrine of withdrawal. Pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world — the visiting and the unspottedness in one sentence, so that separation is not isolation. The monk goes into the desert to escape pollution and takes it with him; the Christian goes into the affliction of the widow and comes back unspotted, because what keeps him is not the distance but the keeping.
roots_summary: Hebrew niddah (H5079), impurity, separation; ga'al (H1351), to defile; Greek miasma (G3393), defilement; alisgema (G234), pollution, of idols.
roots_lines: Hebrew niddah (H5079) — impurity, set apart for pollution; Ezekiel 22:10, Leviticus 15:19, Numbers 19:9.
Greek miasma (G3393) — defilement, pollution; 2 Peter 2:20 only; miasmos (G3394), 2 Peter 2:10.
Greek alisgema (G234) — pollution, of things offered to idols; Acts 15:20 only.
usage: “Escaped the pollutions of the world… again entangled therein” — escape is not cleansing.
“Abstain from pollutions of idols” — the council's first article to the Gentiles.
“Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar” — and the priests asked wherein.

pos: n. (want of purity; uncleanness of heart or life)
etymology: Latin impuritas, from in, not, and purus, clean. The Authorized Version's usual words are uncleanness and filthiness; the confessions and the Institutes prefer impurity.
biblical_def: Impurity is uncleanness, and Scripture locates it first in the heart. “Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?” (Pro 20:9). The blessing is on the opposite: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mat 5:8). Paul's charge to the church is absolute: “fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints” (Eph 5:3), “for God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness” (1Th 4:7). And the cleansing is not self-administered: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me” (Psa 51:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impurity as want of purity; foulness; feculence; want of sanctity or holiness; defilement by sin; unchastity; obscenity in language.
webster_full: IMPURITY, n. Want of purity; foulness; feculence; the admixture of a foreign substance in any thing.
2. Any foul matter.
3. Unchastity; lewdness.
4. Want of sanctity or holiness; defilement by guilt.
5. Want of ceremonial purity.
scriptures: Pro 20:9
Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?
Mat 5:8
Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
Eph 5:3
But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints;
For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
corruption_summary: Impurity is reduced to one sin of the body, and Ephesians names covetousness in the same breath as uncleanness.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:3 puts three things in one list — fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness — and the third has been quietly removed from the modern church's category of impurity. A congregation that would discipline the first two without hesitation will seat the third on its board, and Paul groups them because they are the same disorder facing different objects: the appetite that must have what God has not given. The verse's standard is stricter than any policy: let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints.

Proverbs 20:9 asks the question that decides whether the doctrine is about behaviour or nature. Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? — and the expected answer is nobody, which makes the Beatitude's blessing on the pure in heart either an impossibility or a promise of something given. Psalm 51:10 supplies the resolution: create in me a clean heart — the verb of Genesis 1, used because nothing less than creation will do it. David does not ask to be helped to clean his own heart; he asks for a new one.

The counterfeit is a purity policed entirely at the surface: the filter, the accountability app, the dress code, the vocabulary. These may all be wise, and Job made a covenant with his eyes; but Matthew 5:8 puts the blessing on the pure in heart, and 1 Thessalonians 4:7 says God has called us unto holiness, which is a positive thing and not merely the absence of a stain. A man may be entirely undefiled by anything he has done today and still not be pure, and he will know which by what he wanted.
roots_summary: Greek akatharsia (G167), uncleanness, impurity; katharos (G2513), clean, pure; hagiasmos (G38), holiness; Hebrew tahor (H2889), clean, pure; bara (H1254), to create.
roots_lines: Greek akatharsia (G167) — uncleanness, impurity; Ephesians 5:3, 4:19, 1 Thessalonians 4:7, Romans 1:24, Colossians 3:5.
Greek katharos (G2513) — pure, clean; Matthew 5:8, 1 Timothy 1:5, Titus 1:15.
Hebrew tahor (H2889) — clean, pure; Proverbs 20:9, Psalm 51:10, with bara (H1254), to create.
usage: “Fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness” — three in one list, and the church keeps two.
“Who can say, I have made my heart clean?” — the question that makes the Beatitude a gift.
“Create in me a clean heart” — the verb of Genesis 1.

pos: n. pl. (habitual faults of character; the settled dispositions from which sinful acts proceed)
etymology: Latin vitium, a fault, blemish, defect. A vice is not a single act but a formed habit — the opposite of a virtue, and like a virtue built by repetition.
biblical_def: Vices are settled faults of character, and the New Testament lists them as habits rather than incidents: “the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like” (Gal 5:19–21). Colossians commands the killing of them: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). Their root is not the deed: “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries… these are the things which defile a man” (Mat 15:19–20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vice as a spot or defect; a fault; a blemish; in ethics, any voluntary action or course of conduct which deviates from the rules of moral rectitude; a habit of transgressing.
webster_full: VICE, n. A spot or defect; a fault; a blemish.
2. In ethics, any voluntary action or course of conduct which deviates from the rules of moral rectitude, or from the plain rules of propriety; any moral unfitness of conduct.
3. Depravity or corruption of manners; opposed to virtue.
4. A fault or bad trick in a horse.
scriptures: Gal 5:19
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness,
Gal 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:
Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
corruption_summary: Sins are counted one at a time and repented one at a time, and the New Testament treats them as habits with a root that must be killed.
corruption_paragraphs: The apostolic vice-lists are lists of dispositions, not of incidents, and they are longer in the unglamorous middle than at the shocking ends. Galatians 5 puts hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, envyings between witchcraft and murder, and a church that would expel a man for the first item on the list will elect one who has spent thirty years perfecting the seventh. The grouping is deliberate. Paul is describing one nature with many outlets, and the seditious man and the drunkard are drawing on the same supply.

Colossians 3:5 gives the only method Scripture offers, and the verb is violent: mortify — put to death — your members which are upon the earth. Not manage, not moderate, not counterbalance with a virtue. Romans 8:13 repeats it with the agent named: if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. The Puritans built their whole practical divinity on those two verses, and their insistence was that a vice unkilled is not dormant but feeding, and that the man who is merely restraining it has arranged a truce with something that does not keep treaties.

The modern corruption runs in two directions at once. Therapy renames the vices as conditions, which removes the guilt and with it the possibility of mortification, since one does not repent of a condition; and a shallow revivalism reduces them to a list of incidents to be confessed at intervals, which leaves the habit entirely untouched. Matthew 15:19 is against both: the things proceed out of the heart, which means they have a source that will keep producing, and the source is the thing the gospel proposes to change.
roots_summary: Greek erga tes sarkos (G2041, G4561), the works of the flesh; pathos (G3806), inordinate affection; epithumia (G1939), lust, concupiscence; nekroo (G3499), to mortify, put to death.
roots_lines: Greek erga tes sarkos (G2041 with G4561) — works of the flesh; Galatians 5:19–21.
Greek nekroo (G3499) — to put to death, mortify; Colossians 3:5; thanatoo (G2289), Romans 8:13.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — lust, evil desire; Colossians 3:5, Romans 6:12, 1 John 2:16.
usage: “Hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions” — the middle of the list, where the church lives.
“Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” — the only method offered.
“Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts” — a source, not a series of incidents.

pos: n. (want of moderation; excess, especially in drink and appetite)
etymology: Latin intemperantia, from in, not, and temperare, to moderate, to mix in proportion. Temperance is the mixing of a life in right proportion; intemperance is the loss of the measure.
biblical_def: Intemperance is the loss of measure. Its opposite closes the fruit of the Spirit: “meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Gal 5:22–23), and it is the last of the graces Peter builds on faith (2Pe 1:6). Scripture warns of it in drink — “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18); “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise” (Pro 20:1) — and in food: “be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh” (Pro 23:20). Paul applies the athlete's discipline to himself: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things” (1Co 9:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines intemperance as want of moderation or due restraint; excess in any kind of action or indulgence; habitual indulgence in drinking spirituous liquors, with or without intoxication.
webster_full: INTEMPERANCE, n. Want of moderation or due restraint; excess in any kind of action or indulgence; any exceeding of the bounds of moderation.
2. Habitual indulgence in drinking spirituous liquors, with or without intoxication.
scriptures: Gal 5:23
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
corruption_summary: Temperance is confused with abstinence, and Scripture's word is the mastery of an appetite rather than the removal of its object.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek behind temperance in Galatians 5:23 is egkrateia, self-mastery — power exercised within, over one's own appetites. It is not abstinence, which is the removal of the object, and the difference matters both ways. A man may abstain entirely and be wholly intemperate in what he does permit himself; and Paul, who wrote the word, told Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach's sake. The Reformed have generally held that Scripture forbids drunkenness absolutely and does not forbid drink, and that the vow of total abstinence is a liberty a Christian may take and may not impose.

Ephesians 5:18 sets the two fillings against each other and the parallel is the whole doctrine: be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess, but be filled with the Spirit. Both are a yielding of control to something outside the will; the question is to what. The verses that follow describe the alternative intoxication — speaking in psalms and hymns, singing and making melody in the heart, giving thanks always, submitting one to another — and the man who has never wanted anything that badly has not understood what he was offered.

Proverbs 23:20 attaches the warning to food in the same breath as drink, and the church has been noticeably selective. Riotous eaters of flesh stand beside winebibbers in the text and nowhere in the modern conscience; gluttony is the one deadly sin that can be practised at a church supper without comment. First Corinthians 9:25 sets the standard higher than either: the athlete is temperate in all things, and Paul says he keeps under his body and brings it into subjection lest he himself should be a castaway.
roots_summary: Greek egkrateia (G1466), self-control, temperance; akrasia (G192), incontinence, want of self-control; asotia (G810), riot, excess; Hebrew zalal (H2151), to be a glutton.
roots_lines: Greek egkrateia (G1466) — temperance, self-control; Galatians 5:23, 2 Peter 1:6, Acts 24:25.
Greek asotia (G810) — excess, riot; Ephesians 5:18, Titus 1:6, 1 Peter 4:4.
Hebrew zalal (H2151) — to be a glutton, riotous; Proverbs 23:20–21, Deuteronomy 21:20.
usage: “Be not drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” — two fillings, one question.
“Riotous eaters of flesh” — beside the winebibbers, and absent from the modern conscience.
“Temperate in all things” — the athlete's standard, applied to himself.

pos: n. (a taking beforehand; confidence without warrant; the sin of acting with a high hand)
etymology: Latin praesumptio, a taking in advance, from prae, before, and sumere, to take. The presumptuous man takes what has not been given him — a place, a licence, or an assurance.
biblical_def: Scripture treats presumption as sin with a raised hand. “But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously… the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people” (Num 15:30). David prays against it by name: “Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression” (Psa 19:13). The false prophet speaks “presumptuously” (Deu 18:22), and Peter's false teachers are “presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities” (2Pe 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines presumption as supposition of the truth or real existence of something without direct proof; blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; arrogance; in theology, a groundless confidence in divine favour.
webster_full: PRESUMPTION, n. Supposition of the truth or real existence of something without direct or positive proof of the fact, but grounded on circumstantial or probable evidence.
2. Strong probability; as, the fact is proved by presumption.
3. Blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; as, it is presumption to attempt what cannot be accomplished.
4. Arrogance; as, presumption in a subordinate.
5. Unreasonable confidence in divine favor.
scriptures: But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people.
Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression.
But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.

When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
Jas 4:13
Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
corruption_summary: Presumption counterfeits faith so exactly that men are lost by it, and the difference is whether God has spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: Faith and presumption look identical from the outside: both are confident, both act without visible support, and both use religious language. The difference is single and decisive — faith rests on something God has said, and presumption rests on something a man has decided God will do. The devil's proposal on the pinnacle was presumption dressed in a psalm, and the Lord's answer named it: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. Israel at Kadesh supplies the plainest case: told not to go up, they went up presumptuously into the hill, and were beaten back — the same act that would have been faith the day before was presumption the day after the word changed.

Numbers 15:30 sets it against sin of ignorance, for which the chapter has just provided a sacrifice, and the presumptuous soul is cut off — the Hebrew is with a high hand. What distinguishes it is not the size of the offence but the posture: a hand raised against a known command. That is why David's prayer in Psalm 19:13 asks for restraint rather than pardon, and why he links it to dominion; presumptuous sins are the ones that take over, because a conscience that has once been overruled deliberately is easier to overrule next time.

The gentlest form of the sin is in James 4:13, and most Christians commit it weekly: today or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain — and James's objection is not to planning but to the missing clause, if the Lord will. Presumption in that key is simply the assumption of tomorrow, and the verse gives the reason it is unwarranted: ye know not what shall be on the morrow. The remedy is not anxiety but a sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew zud (H2102), to boil up, act proudly, presume; yad ramah (H3027, H7311), with a high hand; Greek tolmetes (G5113), a daring one, presumptuous; authades (G829), selfwilled.
roots_lines: Hebrew zud (H2102) — to act presumptuously; Deuteronomy 17:12–13, 18:20, 18:22, Exodus 21:14.
Hebrew beyad ramah (H7311) — with a high hand, presumptuously; Numbers 15:30, 33:3; zed (H2086), proud; Psalm 19:13.
Greek tolmetes (G5113) — presumptuous, daring; 2 Peter 2:10 only, with authades (G829), selfwilled.
usage: “The soul that doeth ought presumptuously… reproacheth the LORD” — sin with a high hand.
“Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins” — restraint asked for, not pardon.
“We will go into such a city… and get gain” — the missing clause is if the Lord will.

pos: n. and v. (an infection or stain that spreads; to touch with corruption)
etymology: Old French teint, dyed, from Latin tingere, to dye; crossed in English with attaint, to convict, to corrupt. A taint is a dye that will not wash out.
biblical_def: A taint is a corruption that spreads from a small beginning. Paul twice uses the baker's proverb for it: “a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” (1Co 5:6; Gal 5:9). Hebrews warns of a single root: “looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled” (Heb 12:15). Haggai puts the direction of contagion as a question to the priests, and the answer is that the unclean defiles the clean and not the reverse (Hag 2:12–13). And the whole race is tainted at its source: “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines taint as a spot; a stain; infection; corruption; depravation; and, as a verb, to imbue or impregnate with something odious or poisonous; to corrupt.
webster_full: TAINT, v.t. To imbue or impregnate with any thing odious, noxious or poisonous; as, to taint the air.
2. To infect; to corrupt; as, to taint the mind or the morals.
TAINT, n. A spot; a stain; tincture; infection; corruption; depravation.
2. An infection or corruption of the blood.
scriptures: Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?
Gal 5:9
A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.
Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled;
Hag 2:13
Then said Haggai, If one that is unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean? And the priests answered and said, It shall be unclean.
Job 14:4
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.
corruption_summary: A small corruption is tolerated as too small to matter, and the whole doctrine of leaven is that size is not the question.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul uses the same eight words in two letters about two entirely different problems — a moral scandal at Corinth and a doctrinal one in Galatia — and the proverb fits both: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. The argument is about the nature of the thing, not its quantity. Leaven does not sit in the dough; it works, and the working is silent, and the batch is not partly leavened. A church that tolerates a small heresy or a small immorality on the reasoning that it is small has mistaken a living agent for an inert lump.

Haggai 2:12–13 settles the direction of contagion with a priestly ruling, and the answer surprises every optimist. If holy flesh in a garment touches bread or wine, does it become holy? The priests answered, No. If one unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean? They answered, It shall be unclean. Holiness is not transmitted by contact; defilement is. That is the natural law of the fallen world, and it explains why the strategy of surrounding oneself with good influences never quite works, and why the incarnation is such an astonishment — the one case in which the clean touched the leper and the leper was cleansed.

Job 14:4 gives the taint its origin. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one — the question of a man reasoning about his own birth, and the doctrine the Confession draws from it is original sin: not merely that all sin, but that all are born of a tainted stock, so that the corruption precedes the choices. That is why the remedy is not education or environment but a second birth, and why Hebrews 12:15 tells a church to look diligently: the root does not need to be planted, only left alone.
roots_summary: Greek zume (G2219), leaven; zumoo (G2220), to leaven; miaino (G3392), to defile; Hebrew tame (H2930), to be unclean, defile.
roots_lines: Greek zume (G2219) — leaven; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8, Galatians 5:9, Matthew 16:6, 16:12.
Greek miaino (G3392) — to defile, stain; Hebrews 12:15, Titus 1:15, Jude 1:8.
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean; Haggai 2:13, Leviticus 11:24, Numbers 19:22.
usage: “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” — twice, of a scandal and of a heresy.
“It shall be unclean” — the priests' ruling on which way contagion runs.
“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?” — the taint at its source.

pos: n. (a deception believed; a false persuasion sent or permitted as judgment; rendering Greek plane and Hebrew ta'alul)
etymology: Latin deludere, to play false, to mock — de, thoroughly, and ludere, to play. A delusion is not merely an error but an error the man is being played with.
biblical_def: “And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness” (2Th 2:11–12) — and the cause is given in the verse before, that they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. Isaiah says the same of those who chose their own ways: “I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears upon them; because when I called, none did answer” (Isa 66:4). James warns the church: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines delusion as the act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind; false representation; illusion; error or mistake proceeding from false views.
webster_full: DELUSION, n. The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind.
2. False representation; illusion; error or mistake proceeding from false views.
3. A false belief; a fixed persuasion of what is not real.
scriptures: And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:
That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
Isa 66:4

I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears upon them; because when I called, none did answer; when I spake, they did not hear: but they did evil before mine eyes, and chose that in which I delighted not.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.
corruption_summary: Unbelief is treated as an intellectual misfortune, and Paul makes the delusion a judgment on a prior refusal of the love of the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Thessalonians 2:10–12 gives the sequence in three steps, and the order is the doctrine. First, they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved — a refusal, and note that it is the love of the truth, not merely its information; a man may hold the truth accurately and not love it. Second, for this cause God shall send them strong delusion. Third, that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness. The delusion is not the cause of the unbelief. It is the punishment of it, and it is sent.

This is the hardest form of judgment in Scripture, because it is invisible to the man under it. Romans 1 has the same shape in the phrase God gave them over; Isaiah 66:4 has it in I also will choose their delusions. A God who abandons a man to what he wanted is doing something more terrible than striking him, and it leaves no mark the sufferer can feel. The pastoral use of the doctrine is not to identify who is under it — nobody can — but to explain why arguing is often useless, and why the prayer for an unbeliever must ask for something deeper than persuasion.

James 1:22 keeps the doctrine from being aimed only at outsiders. The hearer of the word who is not a doer is deceiving his own self — the same family of words, and here the deceiver and the deceived are one man. That delusion is self-administered and is the commonest in the church: it needs no false teacher, only a regular attendance and a settled habit of not doing anything about what is heard, and it produces a man who believes he stands where he does not.
roots_summary: Greek plane (G4106), a wandering, error, delusion; energeia planes, a working of error; paralogizomai (G3884), to deceive by reasoning; Hebrew ta'alul (H8586), a caprice, delusion.
roots_lines: Greek plane (G4106) — error, delusion; 2 Thessalonians 2:11, Ephesians 4:14, 1 John 4:6, Jude 1:11.
Greek paralogizomai (G3884) — to deceive, delude by false reasoning; James 1:22, Colossians 2:4.
Hebrew ta'alul (H8586) — delusion, caprice; Isaiah 66:4, 3:4.
usage: “God shall send them strong delusion” — the punishment of a prior refusal, not its cause.
“I also will choose their delusions” — because when I called, none did answer.
“Deceiving your own selves” — the delusion that needs no false teacher.

pos: n. (exemption from punishment or the consequences of an act)
etymology: Latin impunitas, from in, not, and poena, punishment. The word names what the wicked appear to enjoy and what Scripture says they do not have.
biblical_def: Impunity is escape from punishment, and Scripture denies it twice over. Of the wicked: “though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished” (Pro 11:21; 16:5). Of the delay that produces the appearance of it: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11). Of the certainty: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7). And the Name itself closes the door: the LORD is merciful and gracious, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impunity as exemption from punishment or penalty; freedom from injury, loss, or harm.
webster_full: IMPUNITY, n. Exemption from punishment or penalty.
2. Freedom or exemption from injury.
3. Exemption from loss or other ill consequence.
scriptures: Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.
Ecc 8:11
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Exo 34:7

Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation.
But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.
corruption_summary: Delay is read as acquittal, and Ecclesiastes says the delay is exactly why men's hearts are set to do evil.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 8:11 is the most precise sentence in Scripture on how impunity is manufactured. Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. The mechanism is not that men conclude there is no judgment; it is that the interval erodes the sense of one, and the conclusion is reached by the body before the mind states it. Every sin a man commits repeatedly he first got away with once, and the getting away with it did the persuading.

Numbers 32:23 is the plainest denial: be sure your sin will find you out — and the grammar is worth noting, because the sin is the subject and the finding is its own act. It is not that someone will find out about the sin; the sin will find the sinner. Galatians 6:7 says the same in the language of agriculture, and adds the reason the delay does not help: sowing and reaping are separated by a season in every field, and no farmer takes the interval as evidence that the seed has died.

The doctrine is not a threat held over Christians, and the same Bible that denies impunity gives the ground on which the guilty go free. Exodus 34:7 says God will by no means clear the guilty, and Romans 3:26 says how He is nevertheless the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus: the penalty was not waived but borne. What the gospel offers is not impunity but substitution, and the difference is the whole of Christianity. A man who thinks he has been let off has not understood what happened; he has been paid for.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqah (H5352), to be clean, go unpunished; lo yinnaqeh, shall not be unpunished; Greek mukterizo (G3456), to mock, turn up the nose at.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be unpunished, held innocent; Proverbs 11:21, 16:5, 28:20, Exodus 34:7, Jeremiah 25:29.
Greek mukterizo (G3456) — to mock; Galatians 6:7, God is not mocked.
Hebrew matsa (H4672) — to find; Numbers 32:23, your sin will find you out.
usage: “Sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily” — how impunity is manufactured.
“Be sure your sin will find you out” — the sin is the subject of the sentence.
“Will by no means clear the guilty” — and yet the justifier of him which believeth.

pos: n. (a shift or excuse by which a duty or a truth is escaped)
etymology: Latin evasio, from evadere, to go out, escape. An evasion does not deny the claim; it goes round it.
biblical_def: An evasion is an escape from a duty by a device that keeps the appearance of obedience. The Lord names one by its technical term: “ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free… making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mar 7:11–13). Adam evades in the garden — “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat” (Gen 3:12) — and Cain after him: “Am I my brother's keeper?” (Gen 4:9). The excuses of the invited are gathered in one parable: “they all with one consent began to make excuse” (Luk 14:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evasion as the act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogatory; artifice to elude; shift; equivocation; subterfuge.
webster_full: EVASION, n. The act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge or interrogatory; artifice to elude; shift; equivocation; excuse; subterfuge.
scriptures: Mar 7:11
But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free.
Mar 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
Gen 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
Gen 4:9
And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused.
corruption_summary: A duty is escaped by a device that looks more pious than the duty, and Corban was a religious word used to avoid feeding a parent.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 7 is the classic case and its cleverness is the point. The fifth commandment requires a man to support his father and mother; the evasion was to declare the money Corban — devoted to God — after which he was, by the tradition, released from the obligation, and there is no indication the money had to leave his hands. The device was not irreligious; it was more religious than the duty it displaced, and that is what made it work. The Lord's verdict is the most severe thing He says about tradition: making the word of God of none effect. An evasion of this kind always finds a higher-sounding principle to shelter under.

The first two evasions in Scripture set the pattern for all of them, and neither is a lie. Adam's statement is entirely true — the woman did give him the fruit, and God did give him the woman — and it is an evasion because it answers a question that was not asked; God asked hast thou eaten, and got a history of how it came about. Cain's is a counter-question, which is the second-oldest technique. Neither man denies the fact. Both relocate the subject, and every human conversation about guilt since has used one of the two.

Luke 14:18 shows the polite form, which is the one most of us use: they all with one consent began to make excuse, and the excuses are reasonable — a field bought, oxen to prove, a wife married. Nothing in the list is sinful in itself. That is the difficulty with evasion as a category: it is almost never made out of bad things, and the man doing it can usually produce a defensible reason. The test is simply whether the thing required got done.
roots_summary: Greek korban (G2878), a gift devoted to God; paraiteomai (G3868), to beg off, make excuse; prophasis (G4392), a pretext; Hebrew ma'aneh, an answer turned aside.
roots_lines: Greek korban (G2878) — a gift, that is, devoted; Mark 7:11 only, with Matthew 15:5.
Greek paraiteomai (G3868) — to make excuse, beg off; Luke 14:18–19, Hebrews 12:19, 12:25.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretext, cloke; John 15:22, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
usage: “It is Corban… he shall be free” — a device more religious than the duty it displaced.
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me” — entirely true, and not the answer to the question.
“They all with one consent began to make excuse” — and nothing on the list was sinful.

pos: adj. (given to vice; corrupt in nature or habit; faulty at the root)
etymology: Latin vitiosus, faulty, from vitium, a defect. The older English sense is nearer to defective than to savage: a vicious argument is one with a flaw in it, and a vicious nature is one with a flaw in it.
biblical_def: Vicious describes a nature faulty at the root, and Scripture's figure for it is a tree: “a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit” (Mat 7:17–18). The diagnosis is comprehensive: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9); “there is none righteous, no, not one” (Rom 3:10). And the remedy is at the root: “make the tree good, and his fruit good” (Mat 12:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vicious as defective; faulty; not correct or pure; addicted to vice; corrupt in principles or conduct; and, of the will, depraved.
webster_full: VICIOUS, a. Defective; imperfect; as a vicious concord in music.
2. Addicted to vice; corrupt in principles or conduct; depraved; wicked; habitually transgressing the moral law.
3. Corrupt; contrary to moral principles or to rectitude; as vicious examples.
4. Foul; impure; as vicious air.
scriptures: Mat 7:17
Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.
Mat 7:18
A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Rom 3:10
As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one:
Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by his fruit.
corruption_summary: Bad conduct is treated as behaviour to be corrected, and the Lord's figure puts the fault in the tree.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:18 states an impossibility in both directions: a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. That is stronger than a tendency, and it is the sentence behind the Reformed doctrine of total depravity — which has never meant that men are as bad as they could be, but that no part of the nature is undamaged, so that even the fruit that looks good is growing on a tree with a fault in it. The old word vicious carries this better than the modern one, because it means defective before it means savage.

The consequence for method is exact and unpopular. If the fault is in the tree, then behaviour modification is fruit-tying — the practice of wiring good fruit onto a bad tree, which produces an impressive display for one season and no crop. Matthew 12:33 gives the alternative in four words: make the tree good. Only one agent in the universe can do that, and He does it by a new birth rather than by instruction; which is why the New Testament's ethical commands all come after an indicative about what has been done to the reader, and never before.

There is a use of the doctrine that is itself vicious, and it is to make depravity an excuse: I cannot help it, the tree is what it is. Scripture never allows the inability to reduce the obligation — the same Lord who said the corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit commanded men to repent and believe, and held them responsible for not doing it. The inability is moral, not physical: a man does not lack the faculties to obey, he lacks the will, and a will that will not is guilty in a way that a hand that cannot is not.
roots_summary: Greek sapros (G4550), rotten, corrupt; poneros (G4190), evil; Hebrew anash (H605), incurable, desperately wicked; aqob (H6121), deceitful, crooked.
roots_lines: Greek sapros (G4550) — corrupt, rotten; Matthew 7:17–18, 12:33, Ephesians 4:29.
Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; Jeremiah 17:9, with anash (H605), desperately sick.
Greek ouk estin dikaios (G1342) — there is none righteous; Romans 3:10, quoting Psalm 14:1–3.
usage: “A corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit” — and cannot do otherwise.
“Make the tree good, and his fruit good” — the alternative to wiring fruit on.
“The heart is deceitful above all things” — the fault located.
